Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

### tech-news/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.
